Question 1a

Energy: where is the image “busy”?

Sobel · 3×3 convolution

Seam carving prefers pixels that resemble their neighbours. We measure disruption with the gradient magnitude of the grayscale image: strong edges become expensive to remove.

Gx — vertical edges
−10+1 −20+2 −10+1
Gy — horizontal edges
−1−2−1 000 +1+2+1
E(i,j) = |Gx| + |Gy|
L1 magnitude — cheap and robust
gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3) gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3) energy = np.abs(gx) + np.abs(gy)

Implemented in src/utils/filters.py · convolution is done in two separable passes by OpenCV.

Sobel energy · turbo colormap
Bright = high energy = avoid1428 × 968
Seam carving · Assignment 2Energy map
Speaker notes
  • Grayscale luma is used so the energy is a single real value per pixel.
  • |Gx| detects vertical edges, |Gy| horizontal edges; their sum captures both orientations.
  • High energy along the tower and roof means the DP seam will route around them.
Question 1b

DP finds the minimum-energy seam

Optimal · O(mn)
M(i,j) = e(i,j) + min M(i−1, j−1) M(i−1, j) M(i−1, j+1)

Base case M(1,j) = e(1,j). The optimal seam ends at argminj M(m,j), then follows the stored choices back to the top.

Subproblem
best seam ending at (i,j)
Choice
left / middle / right parent
Answer
min bottom cell + backtrack
O(mn) time O(mn) memory Globally optimal Backtracking table

Each cell only depends on the three cells above it, so a single pass computes the whole table. The seam is recovered by walking backward from the cheapest bottom pixel.

Cumulative energy · log scale
White = chosen minimum-energy seamfirst seam
Seam carving · Assignment 2Dynamic programming
Speaker notes
  • The table M stores cost, not the seam itself; a second backtracking pass reconstructs the path.
  • The log scale makes the low-cost valleys visible; the white path avoids the tower edges.
  • Every seam is connected vertically or diagonally, which is exactly what the recurrence enforces.
Implementation

Vectorised DP in the project

NumPy row update

Forward pass — cumulative cost

previous = energy[0].copy() parent_offset = np.zeros((h, w), dtype=np.int8) columns = np.arange(w) for i in range(1, h): left = np.roll(previous, 1); left[0] = np.inf right = np.roll(previous, -1); right[-1] = np.inf choices = np.vstack((left, previous, right)) idx = np.argmin(choices, axis=0) - 1 parent_offset[i] = idx previous = energy[i] + choices[idx + 1, columns]

All columns of a row are updated at once. np.roll supplies the left and right parents; the borders are set to infinity so they are never selected.

Backward pass — recover the seam

seam[h-1] = np.argmin(previous) for i in range(h-2, -1, -1): col = seam[i+1] seam[i] = col + parent_offset[i+1, col]

Incremental energy update

# only ±2 columns around the removed seam energy[:, lo:hi] = _update_energy(...) energy = energy[:, :-1]

Question 2a(i)

How many seams are there?

At least exponential
S(m, n) ≥ 2m

S(m, n) = number of vertical seams in an m × n image, n > 1

1

A seam picks one pixel per row

From column j, the next row's pixel must be in column j−1, j, or j+1.

2

Count only columns 1 and 2

Because n > 1, both columns exist. They are adjacent, so any sequence of column-1 / column-2 choices is a valid seam.

3

2 choices in each of m rows

That gives exactly S(m, 2) = 2m seams. Wider images only add more, so S(m, n) ≥ 2m.

2m is exponential in m. This proves the claim and rules out brute force; DP (next slide) needs only O(mn).

Seam carving · Assignment 2Exponential seams
Speaker notes (~40 s)
  • Question 2a(i) asks how many seams there are. A seam takes one pixel per row, and each next pixel must be in the same or an adjacent column.
  • Since n is greater than 1, there are at least two columns, so I only count seams that use columns 1 and 2. They're adjacent, so every row can pick either one freely.
  • That's 2 choices in each of m rows, so 2 to the m seams. For m = 3, these are the 8 on the right.
  • Wider images only add seams, so the count is at least 2 to the m: exponential, which is why brute force fails.
Question 2a(ii)

Relating a seam to subproblems

Dynamic programming

Subproblem

DP[i,j] = minimum total energy of a seam ending at pixel (i,j).

DP[i,j] = e[i,j] + min(DP[i−1,j−1], DP[i−1,j], DP[i−1,j+1])

Base: DP[1,j] = e[1,j] · out-of-range columns = ∞ · answer: minj DP[m,j], then backtrack.

Why DP works

Optimal substructure: if the path into the parent weren't the cheapest, swapping in a cheaper one would give a cheaper seam. Contradiction.
Overlapping subproblems: each DP[i−1,k] is reused by up to 3 cells below, so it is stored once.

Rows are filled top to bottom: O(mn) time and space, versus ≥ 2m seams for brute force.

Seam carving · Assignment 2Subproblems
Speaker notes (~40 s)
  • For 2a(ii) we use dynamic programming. DP[i,j] is the cheapest seam ending at pixel (i,j). The first row is just its own energy.
  • Every other cell adds its energy to the cheapest of the three cells above it. Neighbours outside the image count as infinity.
  • This works because of optimal substructure, and each value is reused by up to three cells, so we compute it once.
  • In this example the last row's minimum is 5, and backtracking gives the seam 2, 1, 2. That's O(mn) instead of exponential.
Question 2b

Divide & conquer for Sobel convolution?

No asymptotic gain

Sobel: fixed 3×3 work per pixel

Gx-101-202-101 Gy-1-2-1000121 G = √(Gx² + Gy²)

Constant work per pixel → O(mn). Every output pixel must be written, so no method beats Ω(mn).

Divide & conquer into 4 regions, N = mn

Regions write into one shared output (O(1) combine):

T(N) = 4T(N/4) + O(1) ⇒ Θ(N)

Each region copies its own output back (O(N) per level):

T(N) = 4T(N/4) + O(N) ⇒ Θ(N log N)

Verdict

D&C does not reduce the complexity of a fixed-size Sobel filter: at best the same O(mn), at worst O(N log N). Its real benefit is parallelism: independent regions can run on separate CPU cores.

FFT convolution is also D&C, O(N log N), but only pays off for large kernels, not 3×3.
Seam carving · Assignment 2Divide & conquer
Speaker notes (~40 s)
  • 2b asks if divide and conquer speeds up the Sobel gradient. Sobel uses two fixed 3×3 kernels, so each pixel is constant work: O(mn). And every pixel must be computed, so nothing beats that.
  • Splitting into four regions that write into one shared array gives T(N) = 4T(N/4) + O(1), still O(N). If each region copies its output back, that's O(N) per level, so N log N, which is worse.
  • Border pixels also need a one-pixel overlap. So D&C doesn't improve the complexity; its real benefit is running regions in parallel on multiple cores.
Question 3

Greedy seam carving

Local decisions

Algorithm

  1. Start at the minimum-energy pixel in the first row.
  2. In each next row, move to the lowest-energy of the three adjacent pixels.
  3. Never look ahead and never backtrack.
  4. Remove the resulting connected seam, update the energy, repeat.
for i in range(1, m): j = argmin(energy[i, j-1 : j+2]) seam.append(j)
O(m)
seam search
No
lookahead
Local
optimum only

The seam is connected by construction, but a low-energy valley can lead directly into a high-energy wall.

A low-energy trap

cell value = energy e(i,j)

Greedy follows the 1-energy valley into the 100-energy wall. DP pays 9 to detour early and wins: 30 vs 113.

Seam carving · Assignment 2Greedy
Speaker notes
  • The greedy path is valid — it is vertical/diagonal and connected — but its total energy is much worse.
  • This is the classic failure mode: a locally attractive region becomes a trap.
  • On real photographs, the same effect appears as seams that hug a low-contrast patch and then cut through a strong edge.

Speaker notes
  • Does greedy produce comparable visual quality? Sometimes on simple images, but not reliably: it has no way to undo a bad early choice.
  • End-to-end runtime can be similar because energy recomputation dominates; the asymptotic search advantage of greedy is often hidden.

Question 4 · Graph cut

A seam is a cut through a pixel graph

Min-cut / max-flow
1

One node per pixel

Pixel (i,j) is a node. The source s links to every first-column pixel with ∞ capacity.

2

Cutting an edge removes a pixel

(i,j) → (i,j+1) has capacity e(i,j), the cost of removing (i,j). Forward energy |I(i,j+1) − I(i,j−1)| is also supported.

3

∞ edges force a valid seam

Backward (i,j+1) → (i,j): each row is cut exactly once. Diagonals (i,j) → (i±1,j−1): neighbouring rows are cut at most one column apart.

4

Last column → sink costs its energy

Our change to the spec: with ∞ here the last column could never be removed. Using e(i,W−1) lets the seam use every column, like DP.

5

Cheapest cut = cheapest seam

Every finite cut is a seam and costs that seam’s energy, so by max-flow min-cut the seam is optimal: the same objective as DP.

Graph size: V = mn + 2 nodes, E ≈ 4mn edges. Max-flow by Dinic O(V²E) (default) or Edmonds–Karp O(VE²), both implemented from scratch in graphcut.py, with no max-flow library. Horizontal seams: transpose the image.

Seam carving · Assignment 2Graph cut
Speaker notes
  • For Question 4, I did seam carving with graph cuts: instead of building the seam row by row like DP, I turn the whole image into a flow network and find its cheapest cut.
  • Each pixel is a node, with a source on the left and a sink on the right. The edge to a pixel’s right neighbour costs that pixel’s energy, so cutting it removes that pixel.
  • Infinite backward and diagonal edges make sure a cut crosses each row once and never jumps more than one column, so every cut is a valid seam.
  • One change from the spec: the last column links to the sink with its own energy instead of infinity, so it can be removed too, just like in DP.
Question 4 · Algorithm

Max-flow finds the cut, BFS reads the seam

Dinic’s algorithm
for each seam: e = energy(image) # Sobel or forward G = build_seam_graph(e) # mn+2 nodes while BFS(s) reaches t: # one Dinic round DFS pushes bottleneck f along each shortest path: residual −= f, reverse += f S = BFS(s) over spare capacity seam[i] = rightmost S pixel in row i image = remove(image, seam)
A

Level graph (BFS)

Label every node with its distance from s, using only edges that still have spare capacity.

B

Blocking flow (DFS)

Push flow along shortest paths. Reverse edges let later paths undo earlier ones.

C

Read the cut

Once t is unreachable, the nodes s still reaches form S. Every edge leaving S is full.

Numbers in nodes are energies. Coral: source side S and the cut edges · amber: round 2’s path through an ∞ diagonal · dashed violet: ∞ edges.

RoundAugmenting paths foundPushFlow
1s→a0→a1→a2→t, s→b0→b1→b2→t1 + 12
2s→b0→b1→b2→a1→a2→t, via the diagonal810
3t unreachable: stop–10

BFS from s reaches {a0, b0}, so the seam is a0, b0: cost 1 + 9 = 10 = max flow. The two cheapest pixels, a0 and b2, are two columns apart, which the diagonals forbid.

Seam carving · Assignment 2Graph cut · algorithm
Speaker notes
  • To find the cheapest cut, I run max-flow using Dinic’s algorithm, implemented from scratch.
  • In this small example the cheapest pixels are two columns apart, so the flow has to go through the diagonal, and it stops at 10, the cost of the cheapest connected seam.
  • Then a BFS from the source finds the side it can still reach, and the rightmost pixel in each row is the seam. By the max-flow min-cut theorem, it’s optimal, just like DP.
  • [Switch to the app] Scale % to 15, Apply scale, pick graphcut, remove five seams with Step-by-step on: you can see each seam as it goes. DP on the same image gives the same result instantly.

Speaker notes
  • Against DP, the results match exactly: the first seam costs 2060 for both, and all 20 seams were identical.
  • The catch is speed: about 9 seconds per seam against 8 milliseconds for DP, over a thousand times slower, and the gap grows with image size.
  • Forward energy spreads the seams through the sky and grass instead of piling them on the edge.
  • So DP is the better choice for images, but graph cuts handle harder cases, like carving video, where DP doesn’t work.
Three-way comparison

DP · Greedy · Graph cut

Same goal, different guarantees
Dynamic programmingGreedyGraph cut / max-flow
Seam guaranteeGlobal optimumLocal onlyGlobal optimum
Core ideaBest seam ending at each pixel; tabulate + backtrack.Best neighbour in the next row; commit immediately.Min s-t cut = cheapest connected boundary.
Seam searchO(mn)O(m) after the energy mapMax-flow: Dinic O(V²E), Edmonds–Karp O(VE²)
MemoryO(mn) overall; rolling costs and compact parents.O(m) path + energy.O(mn) graph + residual edges.
Visual qualityBest practical choice. Smooth, structure-aware seams.Can be close, but artefacts near edges and traps.Same seams as DP (20/20 identical); forward energy spreads seams more evenly.
Practical speed~71 ms/seam measured here.Fastest per decision.~9 s/seam on 286×194 (DP: 8 ms there).
Best forInteractive editing and production resizing.Previews or constrained budgets.Flexible energy models and research prototypes.
Conclusion DP is the sweet spot for seam carving: the same optimum as min-cut, but exploiting the grid structure to run in O(mn). Greedy trades optimality for a cheaper search and is the only method without a quality guarantee.
Seam carving · Assignment 2Comparison
Speaker notes
  • DP and graph cut both find the global minimum; the difference is the solver. DP is specialised to the grid, graph cut is general.
  • Greedy is asymptotically cheaper per seam search but loses the optimality guarantee.
  • Runtime numbers are measured: graph cut with our own Dinic solver takes about 9 s per seam at 286×194, over 1,000× slower than DP at the same size.
Question 5 · Complexity

Time and space for seam carving

H = height · W = width · k = seams

Dynamic programming

O(HW) time per seam

Visit each pixel and compare up to three predecessors. Recover the path by following parent offsets.

Repeated seam removal

O(kHW) upper bound

Each image is narrower than the one before it.

Overall space remains O(HW)

The image, energy map and compact parent offsets still scale with the number of pixels.

Greedy and graph cut

Greedy search makes local decisions. Graph cut solves a global min-cut; its time depends on the max-flow solver.

Horizontal carving uses the same search on the transposed image. Step-frame storage can require more space.

Seam carving · Assignment 2Question 5 · Complexity
Speaker notes
  • For an H by W image, DP considers at most three predecessors per pixel, so a seam takes O(HW) time.
  • Removing k vertical seams has an O(kHW) upper bound; the width decreases each time.
  • The full program still needs O(HW) space for the image, energy and parent information.

Question 5 · Optimization

Less memory for DP seam search

Same seam, compact parents

Before

Full cumulative-cost table and full parent indices.

After

Keep only the previous cost row and one-byte parent offsets for backtracking.

2.707 → 0.376 MiB traced peak allocations in the finder, approximately 86% lower on this test.

One 500 × 700 synthetic energy map. Memory excludes the input and the rest of the program. Timing is the median of 7 runs.

Source: benchmark_q5_optimization.py · optimization_comparison.csvQuestion 5 · Optimization
Speaker notes
  • The old finder stored a full cost table and parent indices. The optimized finder keeps a rolling cost row and compact offsets, while reconstructing the same seam.
  • For one 500 by 700 energy map, peak traced finder allocations fell from 2.707 to 0.376 MiB, approximately 86 percent. This excludes the input and rest of the program.
  • Overall space is still O(HW). Parallel energy computation may help, but each DP row depends on the previous row and any speedup needs measuring.

Wrap-up

Takeaways

Questions?
DP makes seam search tractable. Exponential seams (≥2m−1) become one O(mn) table plus a backtrack.
Energy is the quality lever. Sobel preserves edges; forward energy can reduce bending artefacts.
Greedy is fast but local. It can be close on smooth images and arbitrarily bad on adversarial ones.
Graph cut is the same optimum, heavier. Useful when the energy model needs flexible capacities.
One engine, two axes. Transpose the image to carve horizontal seams with the same recurrence.
